name: The Frank-Starling Law of the Heart
statement: The heart's stroke volume rises as end-diastolic volume increases, so greater filling yields a stronger contraction.
statementAccent: stroke volume rises as end-diastolic volume increases
meaning: Within physiological limits, the more the ventricle is filled with blood before it contracts — greater preload or end-diastolic volume — the larger the stroke volume it ejects. This is an intrinsic property of cardiac muscle that lets the heart adjust output beat to beat to match venous return.
mechanism: Increased end-diastolic volume stretches cardiac sarcomeres toward their optimal length, which increases the sensitivity of the myofilaments to calcium and reduces the spacing between actin and myosin filaments. More effective cross-bridge formation at this optimal length generates greater contractile force and thus a larger stroke volume.

examples.text: If right ventricular output rises, extra venous return stretches the left ventricle, which then ejects more, keeping the two circulations matched.
After a premature beat, prolonged filling raises end-diastolic volume, so the next contraction is more forceful.
Increased venous return during exercise raises end-diastolic volume and stroke volume even before neural adjustments dominate.

whyItMatters: It is the heart's built-in mechanism for matching output to venous return without external control, ensuring the left and right sides pump equal volumes. It underlies the clinical concepts of preload and the ventricular function curve used in managing heart failure and shock.
limits: The relationship holds only up to an optimal sarcomere length; beyond that, overstretch reduces force and the curve falls off. In heart failure the curve is depressed and flattened, so added preload yields little extra stroke volume and risks congestion. It describes intrinsic length-dependence, separate from neural and hormonal contractility changes.
misreadings: It should not be read as "more filling always means more output"; excessive preload in a diseased heart raises filling pressures and congestion without boosting stroke volume.
origin: Otto Frank (frog-heart experiments, 1895) and Ernest Henry Starling (formalized around 1914–1918).
namedAfter: Otto Frank and Ernest Henry Starling

sources.text: "Physiology, Frank Starling Law," StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf), stating that ventricular output increases as preload increases and explaining the sarcomere length-tension basis — supports the statement and mechanism.
Wikipedia's article on the Frank-Starling law, giving the stroke-volume-versus-end-diastolic-volume statement and the Frank (1895) and Starling (1914) history — supports the statement and origin.
